a: I will not forgive them at all
t: Forgive them, carry them off, or oppose them?
p: The Hebrew can mean "I will not forgive them" or "I will surely carry them off"; the Greek says "I will oppose them".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q79 (4QXIId, Dead Sea Scroll, read as "forgive")
readings.en: that I should indeed forgive them
readings.plain: I will not forgive them at all

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read as "carry off" (the KJV)
readings.en: but I will utterly take them away
readings.plain: I will carry them off completely

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: but I will surely set myself against them
readings.plain: I will surely set myself against them

why: The verb nasa' means "lift", and so "forgive" (lift guilt) or "carry away" (lift and take). Both are good Hebrew. The Plain English Translation reads the line as the last of the refusals in the verse, a promise of no more compassion and no forgiveness.
b: The three children's names make the sense of the verse. The scroll 4Q79 has these words, but its consonants are the same as the Masoretic Text and so do not decide between "forgive" and "carry off". The Greek is an interpretation or a different Hebrew word; no Hebrew manuscript has it.

a: As for the house of Judah
t: The house of Judah, or "the sons"?
p: The Greek has "the sons" where the Hebrew has "the house of Judah".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q79 (4QXIId) shows "and [as for] the house of Judah I will have compassion"
readings.en: and the house of Judah I will pity
readings.plain: As for the house of Judah

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: but the sons I will pity
readings.plain: As for the sons

why: The scroll 4Q79 has the Hebrew words "the house of Judah" in the visible part of the verse, so the Hebrew is old. The Greek has the general word "sons", which makes the verse about all of Israel's children and loses the contrast with the north. Wolff and others think the whole verse is a later Judean addition (see the note); the Greek form is not the evidence for that, since the Greek has the verse.

a: I will have compassion on Lo-ruhamah
t: A shorter line in a Dead Sea scroll?
p: In the transcription of 4Q82 the words "on Lo-ruhamah" are missing; the Greek has "love", as Paul quotes it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and I will have compassion on Not Shown Compassion
readings.plain: I will have compassion on Lo-ruhamah

readings.w: 4Q82 (4QXIIg), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (no brackets mark any damage at this point)
readings.en: and I will have compassion, and I will say to Not My People
readings.plain: I will have compassion, and I will say to Lo-ammi

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: and I will love Not Loved
readings.plain: I will love Not Loved

why: The transcription of 4Q82 has the verb "I will have compassion" and then goes straight on to "and I will say", with no object "Lo-ruhamah". This may be a skipped phrase or a gap that the transcription does not mark; this site has not checked the edition (DJD 15) to see which. Every other witness has the name, and the Hebrew and the Greek both need it for the line that Paul quotes in Romans 9:25. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek translates the name by its meaning with the verb "love".

a: loved by a companion
t: Loved by a companion, or loving evil?
p: The same Hebrew consonants can be read "loved by a companion" or "loving evil"; the Greek chose "loving evil".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q82 (4QXIIg) has the same consonants
readings.en: loved by a companion
readings.plain: loved by a companion

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: loving evil things
readings.plain: in love with evil

why: The Masoretic vowels give "loved by a companion" ('ahuvat re'a), and the next word, "adulteress", makes the woman's lover a man who is not her husband. The Greek reads "loving evil" ('ohevet ra'). Both are possible. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowels, because "loved" fits "as the LORD loves" in the same verse.
b: The scroll's letters are the same, so only the vowels differ, and scrolls had none. Tov notes that the vowels and accents of the Masoretic Text record a later reading tradition.

a: a lethech of barley
t: A lethech of barley, or a jar of wine?
p: The Hebrew has two measures of barley; the Greek has a measure of barley and a jar of wine.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q82 (4QXIIg) reads the same
readings.en: and a lethech of barley
readings.plain: a lethech of barley

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: and a nebel of wine
readings.plain: a jar of wine

why: Lethech is a rare word, found only here, which is probably why a translator or copyist changed it to a more familiar measure. A nebel is a skin or jar, usually of wine. The scroll 4Q82 agrees with the Masoretic Text. The Greek also has "hired" (emisthosamēn) for the Hebrew "bought" in the same verse.
b: The Masoretic Text is supported by a Hebrew scroll and is the harder reading. The Greek may have a different Hebrew text or may have simplified.

a: You must not prostitute yourself or belong to any man
t: A clause missing in a Dead Sea scroll?
p: In the transcription of 4Q82 the words "for me; you must not prostitute yourself" are missing.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q78 (4QXIIc) shows the same words, with "for me" and "not" restored
readings.orig: תשבי לי לא תזני ולא תהיי לאיש
readings.en: you will stay for me; you will not prostitute yourself, and you will not belong to a man
readings.plain: You must not prostitute yourself or belong to any man

readings.w: 4Q82 (4QXIIg), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook ("many days" and "you will stay" are restored; no damage is marked for the missing words)
readings.orig: ימים רבים תשבי ולא תהיי לאיש
readings.en: many days you will stay, and you will not belong to a man
readings.plain: You must not belong to any man

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ οὐ μὴ πορνεύσῃς οὐδὲ μὴ γένῃ ἀνδρί
readings.en: and you will not prostitute yourself or belong to a man
readings.plain: You must not prostitute yourself or belong to any man

why: The transcription of 4Q82 has no words between "you will stay" and "and you will not belong to a man", so the clause "for me; you will not prostitute yourself" is not there. It may be a skipped phrase or damage that the transcription does not mark; this site has not checked the edition (DJD 15). The Masoretic Text is supported by 4Q78 and the Greek, and the shorter text would drop the one clause that answers "prostitution" in 1:2. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.

a: come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness
t: A shorter ending in a Dead Sea scroll?
p: In one transcription of a Dead Sea scroll, "to David their king" is followed directly by "and to his goodness".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and they will come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness
readings.plain: come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness

readings.w: 4Q82 (4QXIIg), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (the words after "David" are visible; "their king" is restored)
readings.en: and to his goodness
readings.plain: come to his goodness

why: In the transcription, "and to his goodness" follows "David" and the restored "their king" with no other words between. This may mean the scroll had a shorter text, that a copyist's eye skipped from "to the LORD" to "and to" (a common slip), or that the leather is broken at that point. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text, which the Greek ("they will be amazed at the LORD and at his goods") also has.

a: your people are like those who bring a case against a priest
p: The Hebrew is hard; the Greek reads "my people are like a priest who is spoken against".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q78 (4QXIIc) shows "like those who contend with a priest" (the word "your people" is restored)
readings.en: your people are like those who bring a case against a priest
readings.plain: your people are like those who bring a case against a priest

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ λαός μου ὡς ἀντιλεγόμενος ἱερεύς
readings.en: my people are like a priest who is spoken against
readings.plain: my people are like a priest who is spoken against

why: The Masoretic Text makes sense, though the grammar is rough ("your people" is addressed to a single person). The Greek goes with a different division of the same letters. Many modern scholars change the Hebrew to "my case is with you, priest" ('immekha rivi kohen), which makes 4:4 lead into 4:5; no manuscript has it. The Plain English Translation keeps the text that has Hebrew support.

a: are destroyed because they have no knowledge
p: The Greek reads the same Hebrew letters as "was made like one who has no knowledge".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q78 (4QXIIc) shows the same consonants for "my people are destroyed" and "the knowledge"
readings.en: my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge
readings.plain: are destroyed because they have no knowledge

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: ὡμοιώθη ὁ λαός μου ὡς οὐκ ἔχων γνῶσιν
readings.en: my people has been made like one with no knowledge
readings.plain: are like people who have no knowledge

why: The verb nidmu comes either from damah I, "be like", or from damah II, "be silent, be destroyed". The Greek takes the first, the Masoretic tradition and the context (destruction in 4:3, 4:5) the second.

a: I will trade their glory for shame
p: The Greek has "I will set their glory to dishonor"; the Hebrew has the verb "exchange".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q78 (4QXIIc) shows the same consonants
readings.en: I will exchange their glory for shame
readings.plain: I will trade their glory for shame

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶν εἰς ἀτιμίαν θήσομαι
readings.en: I will set their glory to dishonor
readings.plain: I will set their glory to dishonor

why: Psalm 106:20 and Jeremiah 2:11 have the people exchange their glory; here the first-person verb makes God the one who exchanges. A change to "they exchanged their glory" would match those verses, but no manuscript has it. This site has not checked whether a rabbinic list of scribal corrections includes this verse, so none is cited. The Greek verb is a looser rendering. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew that the scroll supports.

a: Beth-aven
p: The Greek writes "the house of On" for "house of wickedness".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); in 4Q78 (4QXIIc) only "aven" is visible and "Beth" is restored
readings.en: Beth-aven ("house of wickedness")
readings.plain: Beth-aven

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: the house of On
readings.plain: Beth-on

why: The Hebrew 'awen ("wickedness") has the letters aleph, waw, nun. The Greek read them as the name of the Egyptian city On, Heliopolis. Genesis writes that name without the waw (Genesis 41:45), but Ezekiel 30:17 spells a city of Egypt with the same letters as Hosea's word, and the Greek read it as the city here. A shrine in Egypt does not fit Hosea 4:15, which is about the northern shrines, so the Masoretic reading, which also plays on Bethel ("house of God"), is the likelier. The Plain English Translation follows it.

a: Their drink has run out
p: The Greek of 4:18 differs widely from the Hebrew, beginning "He chose Canaanites".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: their drink has run out
readings.plain: Their drink has run out

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: he chose Canaanites
readings.plain: He chose Canaanites

why: The Masoretic words are uncertain (sar sov'am), but they are the only Hebrew we have. The Greek may have read the second word as a tribe or as "merchant" and so produced "Canaanites" (compare Hosea 12:7, where the Hebrew kena'an means a merchant). 4Q78 has the Masoretic consonants, so the Greek is the odd one out.

a: ashamed of their sacrifices
p: The same Hebrew letters can read "their sacrifices" or "their altars"; the Greek has "altars".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q78 (4QXIIc) has the same consonants
readings.en: from their sacrifices
readings.plain: ashamed of their sacrifices

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: from their altars
readings.plain: ashamed of their altars

why: Without vowels the word is mzbchtm, which can be mizzivchotam, "from their sacrifices", or mimmizbechotam, "from their altars". The Masoretic vowels give "sacrifices". Both senses fit a verse about shame at a shrine; the Plain English Translation follows the pointing.

a: Mizpah
p: The Hebrew word is both a place name and the word for a watchtower; the Greek took it as the noun.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: at Mizpah
readings.plain: Mizpah

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: at the lookout
readings.plain: the lookout

why: Mitspeh means "lookout" and is the name of several places (Judges 11:29; 20:1). With "Tabor" in the parallel line, a place name is likely. The Plain English Translation keeps the name and gives the meaning here.

a: The rebels have made their killing run deep
p: The first half of 5:2 is among the hardest in Hosea; the Greek has "hunters" and no "slaughter".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the rebels have made the slaughter deep
readings.plain: The rebels have made their killing run deep

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: ὃ οἱ ἀγρεύοντες τὴν θήραν κατέπηξαν
readings.en: which the hunters of prey have fixed
readings.plain: The hunters of prey have set a trap

why: The Masoretic Text has "slaughter" (shachatah) and "rebels" (setim). Some scholars read "Shittim", the place of Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1; Hosea 9:10), for "rebels" and "pit" (shachat) for "slaughter". The Greek continues the hunting image of 5:1. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text and admits that the verse is uncertain.

a: speaks against him to his face
p: The same Hebrew letters give "testify" or "be humbled"; the Greek chose "humbled".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the pride of Israel testifies to his face
readings.plain: speaks against him to his face

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ ταπεινωθήσεται ἡ ὕβρις τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ εἰς πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and the pride of Israel will be humbled to his face
readings.plain: is humbled to his face

why: 'Anah I means "answer, testify"; 'anah II means "be bowed down". The Greek takes the second. The Masoretic Text is the same in 7:10. The Plain English Translation uses "speaks against" for "testifies" because the legal language of 4:1 and 4:4 makes the first more likely.

a: a new moon
p: The Hebrew has "a new moon" (or "month"); the Greek has "blight".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a new moon
readings.plain: a new moon

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: blight, mildew
readings.plain: blight

why: The Hebrew chodesh is the new moon, a feast day, and also the month. Some scholars think the original was a word like chasil (a locust) or another word for blight, and that the Greek preserves it. The Masoretic reading is possible: the new-moon festival will "eat" them, a bitter reversal of the feast.

a: walking after a command
p: The Hebrew tsav is "a command"; the Greek reads "vain things".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: after a command
readings.plain: walking after a command

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: after worthless things
readings.plain: walking after worthless things

why: Tsav is the word of Isaiah 28:10, 13 ("tsav la-tsav"), which scholars take to be a command or a nonsense syllable. The Greek reads shav, "worthless things" (the word for worthless things). The Masoretic Text may refer to the king's decree to follow the calf cult (1 Kings 12:28-33) or an order to ally with Assyria. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and says why in the note on "command".

a: His coming out is as sure as the dawn
t: "His coming out" or "we will find him"?
p: The Greek reads "we will find him ready like the dawn" for "his coming out is as sure as the dawn".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); in 4Q82 (4QXIIg) "like the dawn" and "his going out" are visible (the word between them is restored)
readings.en: his going out is as sure as the dawn
readings.plain: His coming out is as sure as the dawn

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: we will find him ready like the dawn
readings.plain: We will find him, as sure as the dawn

why: The Hebrew motsa'o is "his going out" (like the dawn). The Greek read the same letters as nimtsa'ehu or took motsa'o as "finding him". Both lines make the dawn a picture of certainty; only the Hebrew puts the LORD's coming in the dawn's place.

a: my judgment goes out like light
p: The Plain English Translation follows the Greek here; the Hebrew has "your judgments, light goes out".

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: τὸ κρίμα μου ὡς φῶς ἐξελεύσεται
readings.en: my judgment will go out like light
readings.plain: my judgment goes out like light

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and your judgments, light goes out
readings.plain: the judgments on you go out like light

why: The Masoretic Text reads "and your judgments [are] a light that goes out", which is awkward because the verse is spoken by the LORD in the first person. The Greek reading needs two small changes in the letters (mishpati ka'or) and gives a smooth line. This is one place where the Plain English Translation follows the Greek over the Masoretic Text; scholars are divided.

a: like Adam
p: The Hebrew can be "like Adam", "like a man" or "at Adam"; the Greek reads "like a man".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: like Adam
readings.plain: like Adam

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: like a man
readings.plain: like any man

why: 'Adam is both the name "Adam" and the word "man", and the Greek anthrōpos has both senses. A third reading, "at Adam" (be'adam), takes the town on the Jordan (Joshua 3:16) and fits the places of 6:8-9, but needs a different first letter and no manuscript has it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text and discusses the options in the note.

a: murders along the road to Shechem
t: Murder on the road, or "they killed Shechem"?
p: The Greek has "the priests hid the way, they murdered Shechem".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q82 (4QXIIg) shows "priests" and "road"; the verb and "Shechem" are restored
readings.en: a band of priests murders on the road toward Shechem
readings.plain: murders along the road to Shechem

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: priests hid the way, they murdered Shechem
readings.plain: priests hid the road and murdered Shechem

why: The Hebrew ending -ah on shekhemah can mean "toward Shechem". The Greek takes the name as the object of the verb. No scroll shows the key words, since both the verb and the name are restored in the transcription. The Plain English Translation gives the sense that needs no change of the Hebrew.

a: like an oven the baker keeps burning
t: The baker and the oven in Greek
p: The Greek of 7:4 and 7:5 differs in several words from the Hebrew; no scroll preserves these verses.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); no scroll preserves 7:4-7
readings.en: like an oven burning from a baker
readings.plain: like an oven the baker keeps burning

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: ὡς κλίβανος καιόμενος εἰς πέψιν κατακαύματος ἀπὸ τῆς φλογός
readings.en: like an oven that burns for the cooking, from the flame
readings.plain: like an oven burning for baking, from the flame

why: The Hebrew has a baker who stops stirring while the dough rises; the Greek has no baker in 7:4 and ends the verse "from the kneading of fat, until it is leavened". In 7:5 the Greek has "the days of your kings" for "the day of our king", says the rulers "began to rage from wine" where the Hebrew has the "heat" of wine, and has "plague-ridden men" for "mockers". The Hebrew of 7:4-7 is the worst in the chapter and the Plain English Translation keeps it, as the note explains.

a: speaks against him to his face
p: The same variant as 5:5: "testifies" or "will be humbled".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the pride of Israel testifies to his face
readings.plain: speaks against him to his face

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ ταπεινωθήσεται ἡ ὕβρις Ἰσραὴλ εἰς πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and the pride of Israel will be humbled to his face
readings.plain: is humbled to his face

why: This verse repeats 5:5 line for line in the Hebrew and in the Greek, and the same reasoning applies; see the variant at 5:5.

a: They huddle together over grain and new wine
p: The Greek says "they cut themselves", as in a mourning rite; the Hebrew says "they gather".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: over grain and new wine they gather themselves
readings.plain: They huddle together over grain and new wine

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: over grain and wine they cut themselves
readings.plain: They cut themselves over grain and new wine

why: The Masoretic yitgoraru would come from gur, "stay as a stranger", and is awkward. Many scholars read yitgodadu, "they gash themselves", as in 1 Kings 18:28, with a copyist mixing the similar letters d and r; the Greek translates a form of the second verb. The Dead Sea scroll 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves the words on each side of this word, but the word itself is restored in the transcription, so no scroll can be cited for it. The sense "gash themselves" would fit the mourning rites for fertility gods that Hosea attacks.

a: They turn, but not upward.
p: The Hebrew has the odd words "not upward"; the Greek has "to nothing".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); in 4Q82 (4QXIIg) "not" (spelled with an extra waw) and "upward" are visible and "they turn" is restored
readings.en: they turn, not upward
readings.plain: They turn, but not upward.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, as printed in Swete's edition)
readings.en: they turned away to nothing
readings.plain: They turn to nothing.

why: 'Al can be "upward" or "on high" (so "the Most High"), and some read the pair lo' 'al as "what is not", a worthless thing. The Greek read "nothing". The line is a famous crux, and every English version chooses. The Plain English Translation's "upward" is the nearest to the Masoretic words.
